title: Bengaluru's New Gig Workers Wear Cameras on Their Heads. They Are Training Robots to Replace Office Jobs.
excerpt: As coding work dries up, India's IT industry is pivoting to 'physical AI' — collecting the movement data that will teach machines to work in the real world. The pay is $3 an hour.
body:
In Bengaluru, the city that calls itself India's Silicon Valley, a new kind of worker is emerging. Laborers are walking through warehouses, factories, and offices with cameras strapped to their heads, recording every movement — every reach, lift, twist, and placement — as they go about their work. The footage is processed, annotated, and fed into AI systems that are learning to perform those exact tasks themselves.

The pay is around 300 rupees — roughly $3 — for an hour of video footage. The work is called data collection for physical AI, and it is quietly becoming one of the fastest-growing segments of India's IT and business process outsourcing industry.

## The Coding Cliff

The pivot is not happening in a vacuum. It is being forced by the same technology that created the opportunity. Autonomous AI tools like Anthropic's Claude are steadily absorbing the coding and back-office work that powered India's $315 billion IT sector for three decades.

The damage is already visible. TCS, India's largest IT services firm, cut more than 12,000 jobs last year and saw its headcount drop by over 23,000 on a net basis in FY26. Its chairman, N. Chandrasekaran, told shareholders this week that TCS is moving toward having an equal number of employees and AI agents in its workforce. Infosys, Wipro, and HCL have signaled similar trajectories.

The Nifty IT index has lost 27 percent this year. Investors are not pricing in a cyclical downturn. They are repricing an entire industry.

## What Physical AI Actually Means

Physical AI is, at its core, about giving machines the ability to understand and act in the real world. Picture a factory worker picking up a component, inspecting it, and placing it on a conveyor belt. Now picture a robot learning to do the same thing after watching thousands of similar examples.

Teaching a robot is not very different from training a new employee. Before it can assemble products, move inventory, or assist patients, it must first observe how humans perform those jobs. That learning process requires mountains of data — cameras capturing human movements, sensors tracking every action, machines recording how equipment behaves in real-world settings.

India's IT companies are being hired to collect, verify, and organize this information. They are transforming everyday human activity into training material for the next generation of intelligent machines.

"We see continued momentum in AI-powered solutions like physical AI, which is robotics, AI factory," HCL Tech said in its Q3 press conference, signaling that the pivot is now official corporate strategy, not a side bet.

## A $3-an-Hour Workforce

The economics are stark. According to a Capgemini survey, 79 percent of organizations globally are already engaging with physical AI. The data collection that fuels it needs to happen at massive scale, and India's labor cost advantage — the same advantage that built the original outsourcing industry — applies here too.

But there is a qualitative difference. The coding jobs that built middle-class wealth in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Pune paid starting salaries of Rs 4-6 lakh per year. The data collection work pays by the hour, with no benefits, no career ladder, and no guarantee of continuity. It is gig work dressed in a lab coat.

The irony is hard to miss: the same AI revolution that is eliminating high-skilled Indian tech jobs is creating a new tier of low-skilled Indian tech jobs to train the machines that will, in time, eliminate those too.

## The Strategic Bet

India's IT giants are not blind to the irony. TCS's partnership with Anthropic, announced this week, is an attempt to stay on the right side of the disruption — equipping 50,000 employees with Claude and jointly building AI solutions for regulated industries. Infosys struck a similar deal with Anthropic in February.

The strategy is to evolve from writing code for clients to deploying AI agents for them. Whether that transition will be fast enough to preserve the industry's employment base is the trillion-rupee question.

## What This Means for NRI Tech Workers

For the millions of Indian-origin tech professionals working in the US, UK, and Gulf states — many of whom entered the industry through the same outsourcing pipeline now under threat — the physical AI pivot is a signal worth watching.

The skills that earned six-figure salaries in San Jose and Hyderabad are being commoditized faster than anyone predicted. The next wave of demand is for people who can design, manage, and deploy AI systems — not the ones who write the code the AI is learning to write itself.

The camera-wearing workers in Bengaluru's warehouses are the leading indicator. They are doing the work that machines cannot yet do, until the machines learn from watching them do it. After that, the cameras come off. And the workers go home.
